Linear value functions

Describe each state by a few numbers, its features, and estimate its value as a weighted sum of them. A thousand table entries become four or five weights, and moving one weight reshapes the whole curve at once.

The maths

Each state $s$ gets a feature vector $\mathbf{x}(s) = (x_1(s), \dots, x_d(s))^\top$. A linear method estimates

$$\hat v(s, \mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}(s) = \sum_{i=1}^{d} w_i\, x_i(s).$$

The estimate is a weighted sum of features. The dashed curves are the terms $w_i x_i(s)$, and the green curve is their sum.

The gradient with respect to the weights is just the feature vector:

$$\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\, \hat v(s, \mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{x}(s).$$

Raising $w_i$ by one raises the estimate of every state by $x_i(s)$. Lesson 62 uses this to learn $\mathbf{w}$.

With fewer weights than states, no $\mathbf{w}$ fits every state, so the fit must trade states off. S&B §9.2 weights each state's squared error by $\mu(s)$, the fraction of time spent there under $\pi$:

$$\overline{\text{VE}}(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{s} \mu(s)\,\big[v_\pi(s) - \hat v(s, \mathbf{w})\big]^2.$$

Errors in rarely visited states, like the ends of the walk, count for little. Here $\mu$ comes from the expected number of visits $\eta(s) = h(s) + \sum_{\bar s} \eta(\bar s)\, p(s \mid \bar s)$, where $h$ is the start distribution, normalised so $\mu(s) = \eta(s) / \sum_{s'} \eta(s')$.

$\overline{\text{VE}}$ is quadratic in $\mathbf{w}$, so its minimum is where the gradient is zero:

$$\sum_s \mu(s)\,\big[v_\pi(s) - \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}(s)\big]\,\mathbf{x}(s) = \mathbf{0} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \Big(\sum_s \mu(s)\,\mathbf{x}(s)\mathbf{x}(s)^\top\Big)\mathbf{w} = \sum_s \mu(s)\, v_\pi(s)\, \mathbf{x}(s).$$

That is a $d \times d$ linear system, which "Best fit" solves. For state aggregation, $\mathbf{x}(s)$ is 1 for the state's group and 0 elsewhere, and the system splits into one equation per group $g$:

$$w_g = \frac{\sum_{s \in g} \mu(s)\, v_\pi(s)}{\sum_{s \in g} \mu(s)}.$$

Each group's best weight is the $\mu$-weighted average of the true values inside it.
